name: Uma Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the seamer line at a food-canning plant, setting the lid fold and cutting samples open to check the joint. A two-year technical diploma and many years of fault-finding put me among the strongest operators, though the pay is about normal for a lead. I like the clean rhythm of a good run and dislike the noise when a lid jams.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Eva works bakery shifts, and our two school-age children share our mortgage home. We have about four months saved and some similar plants nearby. I use AI every day to group downtime notes, but I check each suggestion against the machine log and the sample can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the canning crew that AI may remain a useful second pair of eyes, but a dented seam still needs a real pressure test. I like a tool that earns its place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The seamer line pays an ordinary lead wage and my partner Eva has a regular bakery shift. We have about four months saved for our mortgage and two children, so a small technology disappointment would not upset the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the lid seam and checking samples each hour. I would keep using my daily AI log assistant for downtime notes, and put a fresh part of any paid weekend shift into our reserve after bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel calm about the line. The school run and the mortgage would still be ordinary work for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check a seam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cut a sample open and measure the fold under a light. A neat label cannot make a loose metal seam safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use AI every day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me group stoppages before handover, then I compare every suggestion with the machine log. I never let it release a batch.

say: I would keep **pressure tests** ahead of software suggestions.
I would tell the crew a **useful tool** has to earn its place.
think: Our **four-month reserve** and two paid jobs cover a short upset.
My **lead wage** stays ordinary for this factory job.
do: Keep **hourly seam samples** and set the canning line.
Use the **existing AI log** for downtime notes.
Save fresh **paid weekend wages** after bills if shifts are offered.
feel: **Calm** about steady work and household bills.
S0.quote: A neat label cannot make a loose metal seam safe.
fieldNote: Uma already uses a **daily AI log** while checking physical seams herself.
Her **moderate reserve** supports calm, and extra saving depends on an actually paid weekend shift.

steps.text: Keep hourly seam samples and line settings
Save fresh offered weekend wages after household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell management that software may take planning and ordering first, while robot handling needs a slower, guarded rollout. The people who know the seam should be paid to test it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The camera could spot obvious dents, and a loader could later take two packing places. I might keep the lead job, but if one person covers both seamers my own hours could shrink; Eva’s bakery wage alone would not carry our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request the new vision station’s error records and run thirty test cans with a qualified technician during an offered paid guarded slot. I would learn to adjust its AI reject threshold only after it misses no unsafe seams in that trial; if my hours fall, I would apply for posted reachable food-line work only where net pay after travel covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about my own rota, though I would rather test the camera than argue from a poster. Thirty cans can teach you plenty if you open them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the trial start just because you asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the plant would have to offer a paid safe place and isolate the reject gate. I would not touch a live conveyor on a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the packers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show them the false rejects and ask the supervisor for written staffing plans. Their hours should be in the trial report as well as mine.

I would keep **staffing hours** beside error figures.
think: A loader may remove **packing places** and cut my own rota.
Eva’s **bakery wage** cannot meet our mortgage alone.
do: Request **vision error records** and test thirty cans if offered paid safe time.
Learn the **new AI reject threshold** after a verified trial.
Apply after **hour cuts** only for posted reachable food work at adequate net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about paid hours, with a way to test the camera.
S1.quote: I would be anxious about my own rota, though I would rather test the camera than argue from a poster.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI habit** makes a new vision-control skill plausible, but she still demands safe physical checks.
Testing needs an **offered paid guarded slot**; any outside application needs cuts, posting and bill-covering net pay.

steps.text: Test thirty cans only in offered paid guarded vision trial
Learn new AI reject controls after verified safe trial
Apply after cuts for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay food job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AGI could arrive in 2028, while capable hands-on robots reach canning around 2031. The recipe sheets may change first; machines moving lids and testing seams could later change the whole crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most checking and loading hours to go when robots can handle the seamer safely. Four months saved and Eva’s bakery wage would not carry our mortgage through a long loss of my pay; I would lie awake over the children’s school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel the planned holiday and ask for written staffing dates. If my paid hours stop, I would apply for posted reachable production or quality work only if net pay after travel covers our bills; if no adequate vacancy appears, I would ask the lender about temporary payment terms before arrears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by a likely large wage loss. I can learn a new control, but the plant may need fewer people to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend the reserve on training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with an actual funded place and a posted job at usable pay. I would keep enough for the mortgage while the children are still in school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Eva add bakery shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She could ask, but the bakery posts rotas only two weeks ahead. I would not put unoffered hours in our budget.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from 2031 physical robots.
I would ask for **written staffing dates** before a crew cut.
think: I expect **most seamer hours** to disappear after capable robots arrive.
Our **four-month reserve** cannot replace my wage for long.
do: Cancel **planned holiday** and request staffing dates.
Apply after **lost hours** only for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work.
Ask **lender** about temporary terms if no adequate job appears.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless school-bill worry.
S2.quote: I can learn a new control, but the plant may need fewer people to use it.
fieldNote: The **physical automation** risk follows 2028 thinking AGI by about three years.
Her applications and lender request depend on **actual lost hours**, reachable posted roles, net pay after travel and possible lender approval.

steps.text: Cancel holiday and request written staffing dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell other leads that thinking AGI in 2031 and capable canning robots around 2034 give us time to learn a better job on the line. A real apprenticeship beats a glossy video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At forty-eight I would still need mortgage income. Maintenance could keep me useful if a local employer posts the work, but I would not leave a paid seamer shift for a course with no wage at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the seamer running and put a fresh amount from each full wage month into savings. If the plant offers a funded, paid-time maintenance qualification with a safe isolated practical place, and a posted reachable maintenance role pays our bills after travel, I would enrol and apply after qualifying; without a place, I would check local operator postings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, but five years gives me time to inspect an actual offer. I want to learn at a stopped machine, then earn at a running one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would practice involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified fitter would isolate the lid feed, then let me replace a worn guide and test the restart. I would need an offered paid place, not permission to watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current shift and compare posted local jobs. I would not pay tuition or leave work merely to hold a certificate.

I would separate **2031 AI** from later hands-on work.
think: The **mortgage wage** still matters at forty-eight.
A **maintenance certificate** needs adequate posted work to be worth it.
do: Keep **seamer shifts** and save fresh full-month surplus.
Enrol in **funded paid maintenance training** only with safe place and adequate posted job.
Apply after **qualification** for that reachable role.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to inspect a real offer.
S3.quote: I want to learn at a stopped machine, then earn at a running one.
fieldNote: Her **adaptive style** seeks a practical qualification but still requires a real paid job.
Course entry needs an **offered safe place**; the later application needs adequate net wages and a local posting.

steps.text: Save fresh full-month wages while keeping seamer shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AGI in 2036 and capable canning robots around 2039 give a family time to learn and save. Employers should pay for the apprenticeships they need instead of waiting for a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be fifty-three when thinking systems arrive and fifty-six when robots may handle lids. The children will be adults, but the mortgage, Eva’s bakery shifts and local vacancies cannot be promised from today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep leading the seamer line and put a fresh part of regular pay into savings after bills. If I am offered a funded paid maintenance course with safe practical work and a posted reachable role at bill-covering net pay, I would enrol and apply after qualifying; in the first year after 2036, if still employed, I would check actual rosters and apply after sustained cuts only for adequate local work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about distant machines while our current money is stable. The long clock gives me choices if real places open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire before 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check what the mortgage and pension figures say nearer the time. If the household needs my wage, I would keep safe paid work rather than choose a date today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you advise the children to join the plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether a paid apprenticeship has an actual place and a job at the end. They can choose their own trade after seeing real work.

I would keep **2036 thinking AI** distinct from physical work.
think: Our **mortgage and bakery shifts** remain uncertain thirteen years out.
An offered **paid maintenance place** could create options.
do: Keep **2026 seamer shifts** and save fresh regular pay.

S4.quote: The long clock gives me choices if real places open.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable canning robots around 2031 could cut most seamer hours while the mortgage still needs my wage. Written staffing dates, funded safe paid instruction and posted reachable jobs at bill-covering net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who tests the first can after a machine change. A family buys what we seal, so I want a person accountable for that first lid.

headlineQuote: A family buys what we seal, so I want a person accountable for that first lid.
portrait: **Uma**, 43, leads a canning seamer with a two-year technical diploma and strong physical quality-check skills.
Her **bakery-worker partner**, two school-age children, mortgage, typical pay and four-month reserve give a modest bridge.
She uses **AI daily** for logs and learns new vision controls only through an offered paid guarded trial.
Fast robots threaten **seamer hours**; longer warning supports funded maintenance training and posted local work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before capable robots threaten most seamer work around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, offered funded safe instruction and posted reachable work at bill-covering net pay would help.
